article.summary: Context OS is a Git-backed context and workflow template for coding agents. It keeps durable context in Markdown and uses shared lifecycle code to produce digest-bound proposals and local receipts for reviewed changes. This review describes selected source at a pinned commit; no runtime, tests, or benchmark workload was run.

sources.label: Continuity briefing and receipt history implementation

who_what.text: The official README presents Context OS as a Git-backed context and workflow layer with Markdown state, provider-neutral workflow skills, and host adapters. It identifies Conor Bronsdon as creator; this review does not infer other maintainer identities.
At catalog ordinal 146, the roster names Context OS, slug agent-context-os, and lists the explicit repository locator. The pinned Atlas item is retained only as identity and locator attribution.

The listed repository is the public upstream; its repository page identifies main as the default branch. The official main feed and commit page identify full head 1a9c688606801de6454a175081d406f47020a144.

architecture.text: The README describes plain Markdown as the durable state layer, with identity, projects, state, sessions, routing instructions, and portable skills. Host-specific commands, hooks, and permissions live in adapter directories; registered runtimes route to the shared deterministic lifecycle kernel.

The documented lifecycle is setup, start, update, and end. Start produces a read-only continuity briefing; update and end create reviewed proposals for state/session changes. The README says accepted proposals are applied with a digest and receipts, keeping the human-facing adapters separate from shared state transitions.

The briefing implementation reads fixed lifecycle sources plus explicitly selected Markdown files. Each source result includes freshness, normalized-text and raw hashes, and an optional expected-revision check; it labels the output a preview, not proof that a host loaded the files.

Git is both the repository format and an important evidence boundary. In split-root mode the README documents separate ContextRoot and WorkingRoot: the former is writable context, while the latter supplies bounded Git identity/status/history evidence and receives no lifecycle files.

behavior.text: Write and update: lifecycle requests are represented as proposals with reviewed diffs and a digest-bound apply step. The README describes setup, checkpoint/update, and end-session handoff flows; the continuity source exposes a read-only briefing and history view rather than writing context itself.

Delete and archival: the inspected README and selected continuity implementation describe lifecycle updates and local receipts, but this review did not establish a general record-level forget API, a deletion propagation contract, or byte-erasure behavior. Those behaviors remain unknown outside the selected paths.

Retrieval: start assembles state, priorities, decisions, and the recent session handoff. A briefing can include at most 24 explicitly selected Markdown sources, only reads regular files up to 1 MiB, includes bounded excerpts, and can compare selected sources against supplied normalized-text SHA-256 expectations.

Scope isolation: in a split-root setup, ContextRoot is the only write target and WorkingRoot contributes bounded Git evidence. The kernel and briefing code use root/path guards for local state. This is a source-level boundary; it does not prove the host permission model or security isolation of a running agent.

Provenance and evidence: briefing sources carry repository-relative paths, freshness labels, and hashes, with optional expected-hash checks. The history view joins local receipts to proposal diffs by digest and reports before/after file hashes, but warns that receipts may be missing or edited, runtime identity is self-reported, approval is not authenticated, and the view is not a complete Git or host read history.

Efficiency and observability: plain files avoid a required external memory database. Briefings bound additional sources, file size, excerpts, and history to 1,000 receipts. The inspected paths expose freshness and revision diagnostics and local receipt history; no runtime telemetry, latency, token, cost, or storage measurements were collected.

metrics.evidence: The briefing path selects and renders context files; no answerability, retrieval-quality, or abstention workload was run.
Reviewed update proposals and freshness/revision checks are source-visible; no correction or stale-value sequence was run.
No deletion leakage or residual-content workload was run, and the inspected sources do not establish a general deletion contract.
Root and path boundaries are documented and implemented in inspected paths; no cross-project or cross-user isolation workload was run.
Briefings expose file paths and hashes; no generated-claim support or citation-coverage adjudication was performed.
No latency distribution was collected for briefing or search paths.
No timed write-then-briefing workload was run.
No provider token usage or cost accounting was collected.
The system uses Markdown and Git-backed state, but no corpus footprint was measured.

limits.text: This is a bounded inspection of the README, shared lifecycle kernel, continuity reporting, and official security/contributor documents. It does not audit every runtime adapter, workflow, operating system, provider integration, or error path.

Local receipt history is not an authenticated or complete audit trail: the source explicitly warns receipts can be missing or edited, runtime is self-reported, human approval is not authenticated, and host reads are not recorded.
The source review cannot establish live host enforcement, runtime scope isolation, correctness of stored context, retrieval quality, physical deletion, reliability, or performance.
No Context OS runtime, tests, or benchmarks were run. The project metric document and fixture define measurement protocol; the shared execution record is not a Context OS result.
